Title: A Retrieval-Grounded and Novelty-Aware Framework for Research Idea Generation using Large Language Models
Hypothesis generation method: retrieval-grounded, novelty aware LLM using scholarly retrieval from Google Scholar, arXiv, IEEE Xplore, GPT-4 and SentenceBERT embeddings, RAG-based generation and novelty scoring
Baseline: sentence-BERT semantic retrieval, RAG generation from top-K papers without novelty-aware refinement, LLM-only generation without external retrieval
Ground truth: no explicit ground truth, novelty is judged by semantic similarity and novelty signals
Evaluation procedure: generated ideas are compared with retrieved literarure. semantic relevance measured by cosine similarity and top-k precision, and novelty is calculated from maximum similarity to prior work and novelty of neighboring retrieved papers
All evaluation metrics reported: Cosine similarity; Top-K Precision (P@k); base novelty score N_base=(1 - s_max) x 100; neighboring-paper novelty; final weighted novelty score N_final=0.7 N_base + 0.3N_neighbor; paper-level novelty based on recency, citation saturation, and GitHub activity; hallucination score H(q)=1-s_max; hallucination rate over the test set. No numerical results for these metrics.
Primary metric result: The proposed framework reportedly achieved higher novelty than the baselines while maintaining semantic relevance, but no numerical novelty score is provided
Baseline result: Lower novelty than the proposed framework; no numerical baseline values reported.
Main evaluation finding/insight: The authors conclude that combining external literature retrieval with explicit novelty modeling reduces redundancy and produces project ideas that are more novel than retrieval-only, RAG, and LLM-only alternatives while preserving relevance.
Evaluation limitations: Performance depends on the quality of retrieved literature and embedding representations.
Evidence location: Section III, pp. 2–4: generation/retrieval framework; Section IV.A, p. 4: baselines; Section IV.B, pp. 4–5: evaluation metrics; Section IV.C, p. 5: quantitative-results discussion; Section IV.D, pp. 5–6: hallucination metrics; Section IV.E, p. 6: baseline comparison; Section V, p. 6: conclusions

Title: IdeaSynth: Iterative Research Idea Development Through Evolving and Composing Idea Facets with Literature-Grounded Feedback
Hypothesis generation method: IdeaSynth, LLM-assisted research ideation system using a node-based canvas to decompose ideas into problem, solution, evaluation, and contribution.
Evaluation technique: Automatic/computational metrics; human evaluation; task-based evaluation
Evaluation procedure: within-subject lab study with 20 HCI/NLP researchers
All evaluation metrics reported: research quality: novelty, impact, specificity, feasibility, relevance; user experience measurements: confidence in literature understanding, expanding research idea, exploring alternative ideas, creating coherent research brief; workload: mental and physical demand, pace, task success, effort required, perceived control, trust in generated ideas, trust in AI responses, trust in literature references; behavioral measures: paper search and reading time, number of papers collected, AI-assisted time, writing time, number of writing actions.
Primary metric: idea impact, idea feasibility, confidence in literature understanding, and sufficient exploration/evaluation of alternative ideas
Primary metric result: Combined MANOVA test showed a significant overall difference favoring IdeaSynth across the four pre-selected measures (F = 3.30, p < .05). Exploration/evaluation of alternatives was 5.40 (SD 1.50) with IdeaSynth.
Baseline result: Exploration/evaluation of alternatives: 3.65 (SD 1.60); comparison with IdeaSynth was significant at p < .01
Main evaluation finding/insight: IdeaSynth helped researchers explore more alternative directions and expand initial ideas with greater detail than the strong LLM baseline. Participants also reported greater task success and made substantially greater use of AI-assisted ideation features
Evaluation limitations: Participants were limited to HCI and NLP, reducing generalizability across scientific domains. Evaluation focused largely on participants’ self-perceptions; the short lab study could not determine long-term idea quality, impact, or research success, and no independent expert assessment was performed
Evidence location: Section 5 “Study 1: Comparative Lab Study,” especially §5.2 Measures and Analysis Procedure and §5.3 Results (pp. 13–16); Figure 7 (key pre-selected measures); Figure 8 / Appendix G (full survey measures, pp. 23–25); Section 6 “Field Deployment Study” (p. 16); Section 7.4 “Limitations and Future Work” (pp. 18–19)

Title: Scientific hypothesis generation by large language models: laboratory validation in breast cancer treatment
Hypothesis generation method: GPT-4 prompted scientific hypothesis generation. GPT-4 was prompted to propose novel drug pairs expected to affect MCF7, avoid MCF10A, and preferably act synergistically.
Ground truth: laboratory experimental response, rather than gold standard hypothesis set
Evaluation procedure: 12 GPT-4-generated drug pairs were experimentally screened for (1) MCF7-vs-MCF10A specificity and (2) additivity/synergy. HSA synergy was calculated with SynergyFinder 3.0.
All evaluation metrics reported: HSA synergy score; maximum-window HSA synergy score; MCF7 specificity / ΔHSA relative to MCF10A; IC50 (µM); cell viability; ANOVA p-values/statistical significance;
Primary metric: HSA synergy score / success in discovering experimentally synergistic drug combinations.
Primary metric result: First iteration: 3/12 generated combinations had HSA synergy scores exceeding the positive controls.
Baseline result: Positive controls: doxorubicin + cyclophosphamide HSA = 1.02; fulvestrant + palbociclib HSA = −2.59 in the first screen.
Main evaluation finding/insight: GPT-4 generated novel drug-combination hypotheses that were experimentally testable and several demonstrated stronger synergy than the chosen positive controls. Feeding experimental results back to GPT-4 also yielded additional positive hypotheses.
Evaluation limitations: uncertainty about whether GPT-4 genuinely “understood” its prompt; some biological explanations were factually flawed; variability across different LLMs was outside the scope of the analysis
Evidence location: pp. 3–8: Section 3.1; Table 2 (p.5); Section 3.2 and Table 5 (pp.5,7); Discussion and Conclusion (pp.7–8).

Title: IdeaBench: Benchmarking Large Language Models for Research Idea Generation
Baseline: human target paper research ideas, Llama 3.1, Gemini 1.5 and GPT families are compared
Evaluation technique: Automatic/computational metrics; human evaluation; expert evaluation; LLM-as-a-judge
Ground truth: research ideas extracted from influential 2024 papers written by human-authored research ideas
Evaluation procedure: BERTScore and GPT-4o idea overlap ratings, GPT-4o blindly ranks generated and target reference ideas based on novelty and feasibility to calculate Insight Score
All evaluation metrics reported: Semantic similarity using BERTScore F1, idea overlap with GPT-4o similarity rating, novelty Insight Score, Feasibility Insight Score, human expert novelty + feasibility ranking, qualitative agreement between human and GPT-4o
Primary metric: Insight Score evaluated for novelty and feasibility
Primary metric result:
Novelty: GPT-4o achieved highest Insight Score in all three domains of Life & Health Sciences, Physical and Environmental Sciences, and Technology.
Feasibility scores were lower across models
Baseline result: No standalone numerical score for the human baseline. The target-paper idea is included directly in each ranking: Insight Score = 0 means no generated idea surpasses the target idea; 1 means all generated ideas surpass it.
Main evaluation finding/insight: LLMs generated as novel as or more novel than human-authored ideas, but performed worse on feasibility. Additional human study showed alignment for novelty, but not feasibility.
Evaluation limitations: Insight Score depends on the number of generated ideas, requiring the same number for fair comparison.
Evidence location: Sections 3.2–3.3, pp. 4–5 (generation and evaluation framework); Section 4.1.2, p. 6 (evaluation metrics); Table 4, p. 7 (main benchmark results); Section 4.2.4/Table 5, p. 8 (reference-filtering ablation); Section 4.3, pp. 8–9, Figures 4–5 (blind human/expert evaluation); Section 4.4, p. 9, Figure 6 (effect of number of generated ideas on Insight Score); Appendix A.4, p. 12 (human-study details).

Title: FoodPuzzle: Developing Large Language Model Agents as Flavor Scientists
Hypothesis generation method: Scientific Agent that uses RAG and in-context learning
Baseline: MolT5 and BioT5; zero-shot Gemini-1.5 Pro, Claude-3.5 Sonnet, GPT-3.5 Turbo, and LLaMA3-8B-Instruct; BM25-based in-context learning with GPT-3.5 Turbo and LLaMA3-8B-Instruct.
Evaluation technique: Automatic/computational metrics; human evaluation; LLM-as-a-judge; task-based evaluation
Ground truth: FlavorDB. For MFP, the ground truth is the correct food category; for MPC, it is the true set of missing flavor molecules, compared at the functional-group level
Evaluation procedure: Models were evaluated on two FoodPuzzle tasks: MFP predicts a food category from flavor molecules and is scored by accuracy after GPT-3.5 judges semantic equivalence to the FlavorDB label; MPC predicts missing molecules and is scored by F1 over their functional groups. Results are compared across domain-specific, zero-shot, ICL, and Scientific Agent methods. Fifty prediction errors were also manually inspected for error analysis
All evaluation metrics reported: MFP accuracy (%); MPC functional-group F1 score. Main Scientist Agent results: GPT-3.5 Turbo: 26.9% MFP accuracy, 0.374 MPC F1; LLaMA3-8B-Instruct: 35.5% MFP accuracy, 0.374 MPC F1.
Primary metric: MFP accuracy and MPC F1 score are treated as co-primary metrics because the paper evaluates two distinct tasks.
Primary metric result: Scientific Agent: 35.5% MFP accuracy with LLaMA3-8B-Instruct; 0.374 MPC F1, achieved by both GPT-3.5 Turbo and LLaMA3-8B-Instruct.
Baseline result: Best non-agent results: 31.6% MFP accuracy with LLaMA3-8B-Instruct ICL; 0.360 MPC F1 with GPT-3.5 Turbo ICL
Main evaluation finding/insight: The Scientific Agent performed better than zero-shot and in-context baselines on both tasks, suggesting that combining domain-specific evidence, retrieved demonstrations, and structured hypothesis generation improves flavor-profile prediction
Evaluation limitations: Benchmarking of the ICL and Scientific Agent approaches was restricted to GPT-3.5 Turbo and LLaMA3-8B-Instruct due to budget. There were also agent error like search space initialization (32%) and epistemic hallucination (26%) and misinterpretation of online sources (20%)
Evidence location: Section 3.3 “Evaluation Protocols” (p. 4); Section 4.2 “Architecture of the Scientific Agent” (pp. 5–6); Section 5.1 “Main Results” (pp. 7–8), especially Table 4 and Figures 7–8; Section 5.2 “Error Analysis” (pp. 7–8); Section 6 “Future Opportunities” (p. 8).
